text: You wake at the edge of a forest. The bark of the trees is a black so inky it's like staring into a void. They are bare, stripped of leaves. Their branches jut out like cracks in the world. Above, the sky is bleached pale—a faded photograph lost to time. It's strangely silent. There are no birds calling. No leaves rustling. No insects buzzing. The air is unnaturally still, as if the forest is holding its breath. You search for a memory. Who am I? Where am I? What happened here? But you find nothing. Instead, a heavy weight settles in your chest, and you feel a pull deep in your bones. A pull toward the forest, like it's beckoning you. You have the sudden, inexplicable certainty that the world will stay this way until you fix it. That somewhere in these colorless woods, the silence is waiting for you to break it. A path cuts through the earth like a jagged scar. Under the thick layer of ash, it feels well-worn and familiar. You start walking.

You exhale, and your breath crystallizes in the frigid air. Pale grey ash coats everything. It clings to your skin. When you touch the trees, the bark lacks the grain and weight of real wood. Instead, it's brittle and paper-thin. It feels like the memory of wood. The forest feels fragile. You press forward.

You find a dry, gray leaf pinned to a tree trunk by a long, smooth thorn. The thorn is driven through the center with enough force to splinter the bark.

You picture someone standing here, driven by a sudden rage, needing to strike at something that couldn't strike back. You imagine them with nowhere else for their anger to go.

You pull the thorn from the wood and tuck it and the leaf into your pack, feeling a strange, phantom heat in your palm.

You continue down the path.

You kick up a stone that hits a massive tree trunk, and a hollow echo rings out. It is a low, thin chime, as if from an empty jar. You wonder if the inside of the tree is gone and only the shape remains. If the world is this empty, what could have filled the space where your memories used to be.

You press on into the greyness.

The trees finally part, revealing the first clear view of the horizon. Far in the distance, a jagged peak looms over the forest. It sits at the very heart of the woods—a towering crown of rock against the blanched sky. A ghostly haze surrounds the summit.

You continue along the path, as if pulled along.

The path dives back into the deep woods. Here, the skeletal trees grow closer together and become pale. Their bone-white branches knit into a ceiling strewn with icicles hung like chandeliers. An icy draft chills you as the shadows of the woods obscure the path.

The pull in your bones is the only compass remaining as you plunge into the darkness.

The forest floor vanishes beneath a tangle of dark grey briars and hardened thorns. Everything here is sharp and interlocking, covered in a frost-like coating of pale ash.

Brittle thistles crunch like broken glass under your feet. Every movement creates a dry, splintering sound.

The scent of dry bark fills the icy air. The bitter cold stings your lungs with every breath.

You push through the brittle thorns.

areaName: Flicker: The Ember in the Ash
text:
A rustle breaks the silence. Something blurs through the charcoal grey thicket—the first movement you've seen in these dead woods.

A creature bursts into view, his four sweeping tails kicking up clouds of ash like pale silk banners. He has a long, slender snout that twitches as he catches your scent. His large, pointed ears stand tall, flicking at every sound.

His face is sharp, lit by eyes that glow like embers. His grin is wide and toothy.

“You're here! I knew it! I knew you'd come back!” He circles you wildly, his four tails whipping through the air. “Hey! {{characterName}}! You're finally, finally back! I've been waiting and waiting and waiting! I followed every single one of your ink trails, hoping you were at the end of them!”

You stagger, the weight in your chest tightening. “I…I'm sorry. I don't remember.”

The creature freezes. He tilts his head, his face falling, and then he grins again. “That's okay! I'll help you remember!” But as you stare at him blankly, he senses your panic growing. “Wait, you don't remember anything at all?”

You shake your head.

He bolts down the path, and you follow.

“Wow, the Unmaking must've hit you really, really hard. I'm Flicker! You're my best friend in the whole world! We used to play hide-and-seek here every single morning. You'd hide in the shadows and hold your breath until I bumped right into you, and then we'd laugh so hard our sides ached!”

Flicker snorts, his breath forming icy puffs, a warm sound in the freezing air. “I don't know why, but you were the only one I couldn't always find. Sometimes, you'd worry that I'd give up looking, but I never, ever did! You'd even leave a little trail of ink just to help me win.”

He trots ahead, his tails swishing behind him. You match his stride.

As you walk, you think back to something Flicker said earlier. “The Unmaking?” you ask him, the word feeling unfamiliar and heavy on your tongue.

Flicker stops and stares deep into the forest, his joy fading for a second. “Yeah! Something super terrible happened,” he says, his ears flattening back.

“I woke up one morning and saw silver flames spreading across the thicket, heading right toward me. Not hot flames, either. Cold ones! They swept through and turned everything cold like ice. We call it the Unmaking, all us forest creatures. When it left, it took all the color from the whole forest.”

Your eyes follow Flicker's gaze toward the heart of the forest, the pull in your bones tugging at you. “Do you know what caused it?”

Flicker starts to shake his head, but the shiver travels through his entire body, leaving his fur standing on end. “Nope! But I bet we'll figure it out together!”

He bounds over a frosted fallen log, and you follow his lead.

Flicker is a blur of energy. He bolts ahead, disappears into a thorny patch. Then he rushes back to your side, his fur coated in frost. “I'm just making sure the way is clear! I don't want to lose you again, not ever!”

He loops back to nudge your hand with his cold nose before darting ahead once more. You pick up your pace to match his tireless stride.

Flicker suddenly vanishes. You stop and look around at the skeletal trees. A sharp yip comes from behind an ash-covered boulder, and he pokes his head out, eyes glowing with mischief. “I finally tricked you! Did you see that? I totally got you!”

He bounds into the frost-blanketed brush, his fur a streak of silver against the gloom. You push through the brush after him.

Flicker stays close to your heels now. “It's been so quiet,” he whispers. He lets out a sharp, happy bark, then another. “I have to keep making noise! Otherwise, the silence is just too uncomfortable. It feels like the forest is up to something it shouldn't be, but that's my job!!” He yips again, a short, rhythmic sound.

The two of you press on through the tall, brittle grass.

Flicker prances in a tight circle, clearing a space in the overgrown brush for you to walk.

“I've been guarding this thicket while you were gone,” he says, his tails held high and proud. “I knew that if I just stayed right here, you'd eventually find your way back to the start. I'm so glad I was right! It would have been a super long wait for nothing.”

He leads you toward a fork in the trail, his eyes constantly scanning the shadows. You press onward.

Flicker stops at the fork in the path. He grins, his sharp teeth gleaming. “I'll keep searching for clues while you go explore! If I find anything, I'll remember it for when we meet again!”

“I'll help,” you promise. “I'll figure out what happened.”

His tails wag excitedly, brushing the ash into small cyclones.

“I know you will! You always kept your promises. It's just so good to have you back, {{characterName}}. I missed our morning games a whole lot!”

With one last yip, Flicker vanishes into the gnarled undergrowth, leaving only a swirl of ash behind.

As the ash settles like snowfall where he stood, the pull in your bones begins to shift. It is no longer just an unexplainable beckoning. It feels more solid now—a resolve to bring back the warmth for the friend who never gave up on you.

You continue, alone once again.

The silence returns, but it feels different now. Less empty. The weight in your chest is still there, but your heart feels fuller. You have a name—{{characterName}}. You have a friend. And somewhere in this hollow forest, there are answers.

You trudge deeper into the woods.

You stop to catch your breath and look down at your hands. Beneath the accumulating layer of ash, a dark smudge of gunmetal grey ink spreads across your skin. You try to rub it away, but the smudge stays—deep, iridescent, and shimmering with a vitality the forest is lacking.

You remember Flicker's stories of the ink trails you used to leave. This ink isn't something you carry—it's part of you. It is a rich and vibrant life force in a world of ghosts.

You pick your way through the skeletal pines.

The trees change as you walk. The ash underfoot is no longer dry and powdery; it has become damp and heavy.

The bark of the pines is soft to the touch, as if the wood has been soaking in a cool, dark lake for years. When you lean against a trunk, it gives slightly under your hand and releases a slow, silent weep of thick grey liquid. The air is warmer and more humid now, smelling of mud and wet stone.

The path begins to flood. A leaden liquid wells up from the cracks in the ground and pools around your feet.

It doesn't splash or flow—it simply rises, swallowing the roots of the pines. It moves with an agonizing slowness.

A low, vibrating hum rises from the earth beneath the stagnant pools, sending vibrations through your teeth and chest. Strangely, it doesn't cause any ripples on the surface of the pool. Neither do your feet as you step.

You force yourself onward.

The tree line thins, revealing a wide, sunken valley. You smell the water, heavy with mineral and silt, before you see it.

Below, the riverbed is filled with a stagnant grey fluid. There is no current, no flow. You can see ripples, but they're frozen in the thick, still sludge.

The pull in your bones is leading you directly toward the water, where something is moving. You descend into the valley.

areaName: Pebble: A Splash in the Sludge
text:
A splash breaks the surface of the river with a heavy, sluggish plop.

A creature scrambles onto the bank, her short, powerful legs moving with frantic speed. She has a long, tapered tail and a blunt snout. She shakes thick droplets from her whiskers.

Her face is round, and her slick fur is caked with sludge the color of iron. From each side of her head, a pair of delicate frills fan out as she breathes.

“Mercy me, I was startin' to get a mite worried! {{characterName}}, you sure are a sight for sore eyes. But I'm ever so grateful you've come back to us!”

She bustles up to you, her dark, beady eyes wide with relief. She paces in loops around your feet as her translucent frills flush with a soft radiance.

“I've missed our afternoon swims in the river more than words can say, dear. We had us a grand time together, didn't we?”

You hesitate. “I don't remember anything. I'm sorry.”

The creature blinks. Then, as if trying not to worry you, she beams. “Well now, don't you worry your sweet head none. If those old memories have gone on a walkabout, we'll just sit right here and make us some new ones. I'm Pebble, dear.”

Pebble slides back into the sludge and paddles alongside you as you walk.

Pebble notices you hesitating at the water's edge. She nudges your feet with her blunt snout.

“It's a mite different for you, I know. You've got those long, land-creature legs. But the water won't hurt you none, dear. It's just nappin' right now. Just put a toe in. I reckon it won't bite!”

You step hesitantly into the heavy grey soup, and Pebble circles your ankles with a joyful whistle.

You trudge along the shallows, the liquid dragging at your skin.

Pebble's head bobs in the heavy river.

“You'd stiffen right up and start to sink like a stone! I'd hold you up until one day you finally let go and just...floated. After that, we'd lay there for hours, just watchin' the clouds go by. You'd tell stories about every single one. 'That one's lonely,' you'd say. 'That one's in a hurry.'”

You look at the stagnant current and press on.

Suddenly, Pebble twirls. She spins in the sludge, her flat tail whipping up in heavy arcs.

“See here? You used to copy me just like this, dear. You'd try to spin on one leg and get all dizzy and fall right over, and we'd both just topple over from laughin'.” She does a clumsy, joyful somersault. “You were a very good water dancer for someone with so many toes.”

You smile warmly and keep moving down the bank.

Pebble flips in the unmoving water.

“We used to spend whole summers dancin' together in the rapids, dear. We'd wade in until you could barely touch the bottom and spin through the spray like leaves in the wind. You said the water reminded you of a story that didn't know its own ending yet: still movin', still figurin' itself out.”

She touches the surface wistfully, and her paw leaves a waxen indentation. “Now the water just sits here, like it just…gave up.”

You continue down the riverbank.

Pebble listens to the low hum from the earth. “The river is holding so much stillness right now. It isn't a bad thing, really. We all need to rest sometimes. I just hope it decides to wake on up again. It's been a long spell, now.”

You walk alongside her, comforted by her perspective.

You glance down at Pebble and ask, “Do you know what caused all this?”

Pebble nods towards the path that leads further into the valley. “I reckon it came from that direction. It felt like the forest took a deep breath in and sucked all the movement out of the world.”

She sighs and looks up at you hopefully. “But we'll fix it! You were always the clever one, dear. You looked at a problem like it was a puzzle, and you never stopped tryin' to solve it until all the pieces fit.”

You and Pebble carry on in silence, the air growing warmer.

The river begins to narrow as the bank becomes steeper.

Pebble stops and looks up at the pale sky. “The clouds are gone today, dear,” she says softly. “But I remember the ones we saw last time we went floatin'. One looked just like a big, sleepin' bear.” She smiles at you. “I think the bear is still there, dear, even if we can't see it right now.”

You both stand there for a moment, looking at the clear sky, before continuing onward.

The river disappears into a forest of massive, bloated mushrooms.

Pebble stops. “I have to stay here and help, dear. Some of the smaller fish are trapped near the reeds. I want to make sure they're okay until the flow of the river is restored.”

An optimistic look comes over her face, and she clasps her paws. “I'm ever so happy you stopped by. Go on now, {{characterName}}. I know you'll find the answer! Stop on by when you do.”

With a determined whistle, she twirls and dives back into the sludge. The sound of her whistle lingers longer than it should.

The pull in your bones is overshadowed by your desire to restore the river for the friend who never let you sink.

You continue alone down the path.

The air changes. The muddy scent of the river is replaced by something sweet and cloying, like rotten earth and ancient decay.

The air becomes sticky, the river widens, and the ground changes into a viscous muck, grasping at your feet as you walk.

You force yourself to keep moving.

In the shadow of a bloated mushroom, you find a thick vine tied into a ball of impossible, tight knots. Someone must have pulled these so hard that the vine has cut into itself repeatedly.

You picture someone yanking on these in frustration, trying to untangle them. You imagine them wanting so desperately to move forward but only binding themselves tighter with every attempt to break free.

You tuck the gnarled ball into your pack. It is an unyielding knot that no amount of patience can undo.

The muck rises to your ankles, and you struggle to continue.

You stop in the middle of the sticky mire, your breath coming in ragged gasps as the humidity of the marsh settles over you. You look at the dark smudge on your skin and remember Pebble's words—how you once said the water reminded you of a story that didn't know its own ending yet. Here, in a world that has completely stalled, you realize that you are like that unstoppable current. You have no memories, no beginning you can point to, no sense of what comes next. And yet something in you keeps moving forward anyway. You wipe the sweat and ash from your brow and trudge toward a line of massive, pale shapes on the horizon.

You find a heavy root segment half-buried in the riverbank's mire. It has grown around a dull, metallic nugget, trapping the weight inside.

You picture someone letting this sink into the mud, watching as the heaviness pulled it under. You imagine them feeling as if they were drowning under the weight of their own despair. You pull the leaden root from the muck and drop it into your bag. It thuds heavily.

You walk toward a clearing, where the trees finally end.

The valley has fully surrendered to the marshland. Massive mushrooms tower over the path, their colors bled dry into shades of grey, their caps weeping black ooze.

A sickly scent of rot hangs in the muggy air. The cycles of life here seem to have jammed halfway through—nothing grows, and nothing fully disappears.

Everything is stuck in a state of eternal, frustrated decay. You trudge into the heart of the rot.

areaName: Gully: The Chorus of the Marsh
text: A deep, resonant croak vibrates through the colorless stalks. A large reptilian creature with bumpy, leathery skin and pale, bulbous spots across his back sits atop a pearly shelf fungus. He has three wide, heavy-lidded eyes. The middle one centered in his forehead is a pupilless, milky white. His broad mouth seems permanently curled into a relaxed grin. As he speaks, his throat—a wide vocal sac translucent as frosted glass—pulses with a bioluminescent radiance. “Oooooooh, look at that. The rhythm has returned.” He doesn't hop so much as he tiptoes with a strange, rhythmic grace. “{{characterName}}! You're back! I've been practicing the songs we used to sing together, though the acoustics in this rot are...well, a bit muffled.” You explain that your memory is gone. You don't remember him or even yourself. The creature lets out a wet, musical chuckle, the light in his throat swirling like smoke. “That's okay. I'm Gully. And you're an Inker, friend. You aren't just in the world—the world is of you. You're the one who gives the forest its substance. Its weight. Without you, all of this is just a sketch waiting for someone to turn it into a work of art.” You step back onto the sticky path, and Gully follows with a slow grace, his vocal sac pulsing a steady glow.

Gully stops to look at a cluster of tadpoles suspended above a stagnant pool. They are frozen midjump, their tails translucent and iridescent. Nearby, a dead leaf hangs halfway between a branch and the mud, caught in an unmoving mist. “Everything got stuck,” Gully says, his voice a melodic ribbit. “The Unmaking didn't just take the color—it took the next. Tadpoles can't grow. Leaves can't become soil. It's like the marsh just stopped midsentence.” You push past a weeping mushroom, the air growing denser, as Gully hops beside you.

Gully nudges a mushroom cap with his webbed toe, and instead of releasing spores, it simply weeps a single, thick drop of black goo.

“The cycles are jammed. It's a frustrating tune to listen to, honestly. An unfinished song, if you will.”

You trudge onward while Gully tiptoes through the viscous, smoky grey mire.

As you walk, Gully begins to hum a low, rumbling note.

“You know, the mushrooms used to glow when you passed —a warm glow that filled the whole bog. We'd search for the ones that glowed the brightest,” he says, his eyes drifting to the dull caps around you. “Not because you touched them. Just because you were near.”

He watches you for a moment. “They don't do that for anyone else. I've been here a long time. I would know.”

His hum vibrates in your chest as you navigate together between the giant, dull stalks.

Gully looks at you, his eyes unblinking, the center one seeming to perceive something otherwise invisible.

“We used to jam all the time. I provided the rhythm; you provided the melody. We were a perfect harmony, you and me. I don't know why the song ended, {{characterName}}, but I'm glad you're here to hear the silence with me. It's much less lonely with two.”

You push through a curtain of weeping moss, Gully's steady, unhurried hopping keeping pace beside you.

Gully pauses and his throat pulses in a slow, heavy rhythm.

“It came from that way,” he says softly, pointing a webbed finger deeper into the marsh, his milky eye focused on something you cannot see.

“Instantly, everything started to turn. All the mushrooms started turning to goo and dripped into the peat. The wood started decaying, going soft and black. Everything started rotting.”

You both walk toward the distant haze, the unease of the story settling over you.

Gully sighs, a sound of wet gravel.

“But then the transformation just didn't finish. The Unmaking stopped everything halfway through. The rot started but couldn't complete. Now everything is stuck between states—too dead to live, but not dead enough to become something new. It's like the forest is holding its breath, waiting for something that never comes.”

The muggy air is replaced by a dry, biting breeze as you and Gully walk toward the edge of the wetlands.

The ground is becoming firmer, the cloying smell of decay starting to thin. The giant mushrooms are still tall, but they are fewer and further between.

Gully stops at the edge of a cluster of weeping caps. “The mycelium—the network under the dirt—it's feeling a little jammed up here. I'm gonna hang back for a bit and feed the roots a little frequency. Keep the network from going totally quiet.”

He looks at you curiously, his third eye squinting, as if trying to make out something faint.

“Go on, {{characterName}}. Our grooves are locked in now. You find what's stopping the tune; I'll keep the low end steady in the mud. I'll be right here if the beat starts to slip.”

With one final, deep croak, Gully settles into the mud.

As his croak echoes and then falls silent, the pull in your bones begins to play second fiddle to your determination to bring the forest's music back for the friend who made your life sing.

You continue alone, the damp silence of the marsh settling over you once more.

As you leave Gully behind, the sickeningly sweet smell of the marsh begins to fade. The air loses its humid weight and is replaced by a thin breeze that smells of mineral and ozone.

The mushrooms here are shrunken and withered. Their caps curl inward like dried fruit as they withdraw into the darkening mud.

The muck on the path is starting to thin, revealing the unyielding rock beneath.

You walk toward the lengthening shadows of the boulders ahead.

The ground under your feet is changing.

The viscous, grasping peat is drying out, turning into a cracked and thirsty stone. Every step no longer produces a wet suction, but a dry, muffled thud.

The trees are returning, but now they're stunted, ashen pines with razor-sharp needles. Their roots claw into the stone like desperate fingers.

You pick your way across the parched earth as the slope begins to tilt upward.

You find a smooth stone in the dirt with a deep groove worn into its center. Someone must have held it often, rubbing their thumb against the surface until the rock gave way.

You picture someone carrying a weight of terror they couldn't name, seeking comfort in the repetitive motion of their hand. You imagine them fearing that they were truly, fundamentally alone.

The stone is heavy in your hand, yet it feels light compared to the leaden weight in your chest. You take it with you.

You continue toward the looming rock wall, an icy breath of wind causing goosebumps on your inky skin.

You stop for a moment, looking back at the distant, gloomy smudge of the wetlands. You think about what Gully said—that the world is just a sketch waiting for someone to turn it into a work of art. You look at your hands, at the ink that shimmers beneath the ash, and realize he was talking about you. The forest is the canvas, and you are the medium. The stillness around you is a vast, empty space, and the urge to fill it—to make something substantial out of this void—pulses in your blood like a second heartbeat. You turn away from the wetlands and approach the dark, yawning entrance at the foot of a mountain.

The path leads directly into the base of a mountain, where the parched earth gives way to cold, craggy stone.

You step into a vast network of caves. Great crystal formations jut from the walls like frozen lightning, but they are cracked and dim, their light long since extinguished.

The air smells metallic and silty. An unbearable pressure seems to press down from the ceiling, making it difficult to breathe.

It feels as if the cave walls themselves are closing in around you.

You take a moment to slow your breathing before stepping into the darkness of the caverns.

A wet sniffle cuts through the silence.

A tiny figure hangs by their feet from a high, jagged outcropping, two black eyes absorbing what little light remains.

Their wings are wrapped tightly around them like a cocoon of thin, translucent silk. It shrouds their small, fragile body in a silvery sheath.

They have velvety fur the color of silver. Their nose is broad and blunt, pressed flat against their face like a thumbprint.

Their ears are exceptionally large, twitching with a mechanical precision as they catch the sound of your footsteps.

“S-s-subject is thirty-four days late,” the creature says, their voice small but clipped. “The error margin is grotesque.”

You stop beneath the outcropping and look up at the shrouded form. “I'm sorry. I forgot,” you say. “I forgot everything.”

The figure releases their grip and begins to drift in a wide circle around you. Their wings unfurl and ripple behind them in long, slow arcs like a scholar's robes suspended in water as they study you.

The creature sniffs quietly, their nose twitching as they record the scent—ink. Faded but unmistakable.

“Anomalous,” the creature says, sharply and clinically, banking around a dim crystal.

“The Unmaking has rendered the world's data unreliable. I am Mica. I have spent eons documenting the magnetic and acoustic properties of this s-s-strata. To understand the world's s-s-structure is the only way to be truly free. Your amnesia is a catastrophic loss of data. We must proceed. Maintain a three-meter buffer to prevent proximity interference.”

Mica drifts ahead, a silvery shape dissolving into the dark. You move to keep them in sight.

The air here is thick and heavy. It presses against your chest with a crushing force that makes every breath feel labored.

Mica glides through the dense atmosphere, their ears independently rotating to track the smallest vibrations in the stone. A soft sneeze shakes their small frame, and they twitch their ears in annoyance at the interruption.

“Archive data indicates a s-s-systemic overwrite,” Mica says, their eyes scanning the deep cracks that splinter across the cavern walls like lightning.

“The Unmaking applied a crushing pressure that has compromised the integrity of these s-s-structures. It is a faulty environment. The world requires a s-s-stable anchor to resist the weight. In simpler terms—when everything around you is changing, you need certainty and stability, or you lose track of what is real.”

You press forward, following the steady beat of Mica's wings.

The path tightens, and the pressure intensifies until the silence feels like a physical weight on your eardrums.

You move to step alongside Mica, but the creature flinches. Their large ears pin back against their skull as they swerve sharply away.

They shudder, their breath momentarily shaky and their wings rippling in a tight, agitated pulse until the three-meter gap is restored.

“Maintain the buffer,” Mica commands, their voice strained.

“Your presence creates a localized distortion in the s-s-spatial data. If you move too close, your acoustic signature is too intense for close-range monitoring. The proximity is insufficient.”

Mica pulls ahead without looking back. You match their pace through the dark.

The cavern opens into a series of rounded chambers where the walls are pockmarked with shallow, jagged holes.

Mica circles the room, their ears twitching at the sound of the rock groaning under the pressure. They pause, looking at the ceiling where the stone bows inward.

“Chronological logs identify this chamber as the site of Experiment 1: Acoustic Resonance Mapping,” Mica says, their voice muffled and clipped in the dense air. “In the past, you provided an acoustic trigger, and I utilized the return to construct a s-s-spatial map. The air density was lower then. Currently, the particulate s-s-saturation is absorbing the acoustic return before it can travel. Try to replicate the hum.”

Mica drifts to the far edge of the chamber. You move deeper into the dark after them.

Per Mica's instruction, you let out a low, steady note, but the sound feels like it is being choked as soon as it leaves your throat. It does not travel; it simply hangs in the thick air for a moment before dropping away.

Mica's ears twitch, catching the lack of return. “S-s-signal is absent. This does not match the archival data from our previous s-s-sessions. In the past, the transformation of the stone was instantaneous. In other words, you could shape the world with your voice. Currently, however, your output is below the required threshold. The resonance is ineffective.”

Mica sniffles and records the failure.

Mica turns and glides onward, wings barely rippling. You fall into step beneath them.

Mica suddenly lets out a wet, high-pitched sneeze that causes them to wobble in the air. Their wings churn in a frantic surge to regain their hover, and they look physically drained by the effort of maintaining their flight in the thick air.

With a quick shake, they settle their ruffled fur. “The particulate matter from the crumbling s-s-stone is a persistent allergen,” Mica mutters, eyes watery and narrowed.

“Physically, this environment is taxing for a vessel of my s-s-size. However, my mental faculties remain s-s-stable. Knowledge is the only liberation from the s-s-suffering of the flesh.”

Mica steadies, soars higher, and presses on. You walk beneath them through the settling dust.

You continue through the gallery of fractured chambers, where the crushing weight seems to grow heavier with every step.

You ask Mica if anything else changed when you disappeared.

Mica circles a stalactite, their movements structured and precise. “Affirmative,” Mica replies, their ears rotating back toward you.

“The previous recordings include an observation outside the formal experimental parameters. In the past, the s-s-shadows in this chamber behaved anomalously in your presence. Their angles did not correspond to any fixed light s-s-source. I have no satisfactory explanation for the data. I recorded it regardless.”

Mica glides silently into the next passage. You follow the faint shimmer of their wings.

The path drops into a shallow depression filled with silver dust and crushed rock.

As you walk, your foot strikes something hard and metallic under crumbled stone. You reach down and pull a tarnished metal compass from the debris. It is heavy and cold, the glass cracked from the weight of the stone. The needle spins in frantic, meaningless circles.

Mica drifts closer, their eyes glowing with a faint, shifting light.

“Ah,” Mica says, their voice dropping lower, as if describing a precious artifact.

“That is the property of the s-s-strata. I had recorded it as lost during the inventory following the Unmaking. It is a precision instrument, designed to track the subsurface field lines when the atmosphere is too thick for s-s-sensory mapping.”

You continue through the silver dust, turning the tarnished metal over in your hands.

The air begins to thrum with a low, electric tension as you enter a massive vault.

Mica glides toward the center, their wings shimmering as they sense the magnetic lines. They sniffle and then clear their throat grandly.

“Observe Experiment 2: Magnetic Field Line Mapping. I loaned you that device...” Mica says, gesturing at the compass, “..to verify the accuracy of my magnetoreceptive readings. We recorded the coordinates of the s-s-subsurface field lines while I traced their paths through the rock. When you went missing, the lines became fractured. They drifted through the s-s-stone without a guide. Now, analyze the needle.”

You look down at the compass. It has stopped spinning. It points directly at your chest.

Mica circles the vault in a slow, wide arc. You walk beneath them, the compass heavy in your hand.

As you move across the chamber, the needle of the compass follows you with mechanical precision. Every step you take realigns the magnetic orientation of the entire vault, the invisible field lines bending toward you despite the crushing weight of the atmosphere.

“S-s-scientifically impossible. Magnetic North has always tracked your position. I recorded it myself. When you disappeared, it had nothing to follow, and the needle simply s-s-spun. But you have returned, and it is recalibrating to you again. You are the anchor point for a world under pressure. The world is rewriting its own compass to point at you.”

Mica ascends toward the passage above. You trudge upward after them.

Mica doesn't fly ahead this time. They stay beside you, exactly three meters away, maintaining a steady hover that keeps them in your peripheral vision.

Whenever you turn your head toward them, Mica's ears flick backward, and they drift a few inches further away, as if your direct attention is physically loud.

“Close-range monitoring is required to observe the way the field lines react to your gait,” Mica says. “It is a s-s-substantial amount of data. It would be insufficient for me to be elsewhere when the s-s-subject is so active. The electromagnetic overlap is manageable.”

Mica remains exactly three meters to your left as you move toward the final cluster of crystals.

The path is lined with massive, clouded crystals. They are dull and smoky, their surfaces covered in a thick layer of ash and deep cracks. Mica hovers near a jagged crack in a central pillar and sweeps one wing out ceremoniously toward a cluster of crystals.

“Experiment 3: Crystalline Lattice Alignment,” Mica says. “In the past, you touched the crystals to repair their s-s-structural integrity. They would realign under your touch. Now, they are crumbling under the weight of the Unmaking. Contact is necessary for recalibration.”

You approach the clouded stones.

You reach out and press your palm against the largest crystal, hoping to feel the stone smooth out as Mica described. A deep, iridescent shimmer pulses from your hand, and for a moment, the internal lattice of the crystal clicks.

A single crack begins to seal itself, and a spark of sharp light flares in the center. But as quickly as it began, the shimmer fades. The light flickers and dies, leaving the crystal as dull and clouded as before.

Mica's ear twitches as they record the failure. “The internal lattice remains fractured. S-s-stability is not restored. The ink is failing to act as a binder, unlike our previous s-s-sessions. You used to be able to heal the world with your touch. The capacity is not absent—it is dormant. The data is inconclusive as to why.”

Mica drifts away from the crystals. You trail them, leaving the dim stones behind.

The cavern remains dark, the colorless ash on the ground swallowing the little light you have left.

Mica hovers nearby, their fur flattened by the heavy air. They look at you, their head tilting at a sharp angle.

“The s-s-stability has not returned,” Mica observes. “The Unmaking continues to unbind the laws of physics here, though your presence prevents total collapse. You are the reason this place hasn't collapsed into a s-s-single point, even if you cannot yet repair the damage. Knowledge of this fact is a s-s-step toward freedom.”

Mica turns and heads toward the faint light above. You follow, your feet stirring ash with every step.

As you climb, the air becomes thinner and the crushing pressure begins to lift. The jagged floor turns back into dark, damp loam covered in thick mats of spongy moss and powdery lichen. You can see the light of the pale moon through the narrow exit above.

Mica glides ahead, their wings undulating slowly in the night air. They sniffle again, the sound louder, less muffled than before.

“The s-s-surface conditions are within acceptable parameters,” Mica reports. “Prepare for the change in density. The s-s-space ahead is much less confined. It will be a s-s-significant shift in your sensory input, but my recordings suggest you handle the transition well.”

Mica ripples upward through the thinning air. You climb the final incline.

The path reaches the exit, looking out over a distant, moonlit grove. A dim crescent moon hangs low in the sky, barely brushing the tops of the trees.

Before you can turn away, Mica reaches out a small, bone-white claw and plucks the tarnished metal compass from your hand.

“That belongs to me,” Mica says, their voice small. “I must remain here. The new data requires s-s-sorting. I must map the new baseline of this forest. You have provided a s-s-substantial s-s-sample of your influence, {{characterName}}. It matches my prior records of your identity, although it is s-s-significantly diminished.”

Mica tilts their head, their dark eyes fixed on your silhouette against the bright exit. “You are distinct from the other creatures of this s-s-strata. Such a difference brings with it great power, and with that power comes great responsibility. It is your duty to help the world understand itself once more, even if you do not yet feel you are s-s-suited for the role.”

You look at the creature. “Will you be okay here?”

“I have my observations,” Mica says, settling their ears against the stone. “Go. The s-s-subject must continue to move if the data is to remain relevant to the world's s-s-salvation.”

Mica stops at the mouth of the cave, hanging upside-down once again from a low rock. They wrap their silk-like wings back around their small frame, becoming a still, silvery shroud once more.

As the cave entrance shrinks behind you, the pull in your bones finds a new gravity. It is no longer just an instinctual drift, but a determination to restore the order of the world for the friend who dedicated their days to learning everything about you and the world you helped shape.

You step out of the cave and into the night air.

The trees change as you walk. They are no longer standing straight; they are bent and gnarled, frozen mid-contortion. Their branches reach deeper into the forest in tangled spirals, as if desperate. They look like they froze in the middle of a struggle, trying to grab hold of something they can no longer reach.

As you navigate through the wreckage, you feel the brittle branches brushing against your shoulders and arms, as if the trees are still trying to pull you toward them. When you pass them, you hear a faint, high-pitched creak, like the groan of a sinking ship.

You move quickly to clear the reach of the wood.

You find a piece of white bark from a fallen tree. Two figures are drawn in charcoal, their arms linked in camaraderie. But then someone used a piece of coal to grind one of the figures into a black scribble, scratching them out completely.

You picture someone watching from the shadows, unable to bear seeing others have what they lacked. You imagine them desperately trying to erase a happiness they coveted.

You pick up the bark and the fragment of coal, feeling the soot lingering, staining your fingers.

You continue through the dark woods.

Mica's clinical parting words carry a weight that persists even as the cave air thins. They spent their days recording a world that was falling apart, but they saw you as the only coordinate that remained fixed.

Now that you have seen how the laws of the forest behave—how the very logic of the world shifts to track your presence—the ignorance you woke with feels like a luxury you've lost. This knowledge is a duty.

You were the only one who could understand the structure of the world you've returned to. And you are the only one who can repair it.

It is your responsibility to help the creatures and undo the damage of the Unmaking.

You walk toward the sound of rustling leaves ahead.

The stone path finally softens, disappearing into a towering cathedral of ancient oaks. These are not the spindly, broken trees from the forest's edge; they are massive and imposing. Their wide trunks are wrapped in bark so deeply furrowed it looks like weathered iron.

High above, the canopy is a dense, interlocking weave of branches. Yet, the leaves are brittle—mere silhouettes against the hollow sky.

The air is damp and smells of wet bark, and the sky is a vast, starless expanse. Every star has been plucked from the dark, leaving the space between the clouds empty.

The moon has climbed higher since you left the caverns, but its light is too thin and diminished to illuminate your path. It hangs like a fading ember in the blackness, casting a dim, silvery shadow that barely reaches the forest floor. The darkness here feels like a hole in the world where something used to be.

The only sound is the dry, rhythmic rasp of oak limbs shifting in the high-altitude air. You stand at the center of the grove, a solitary figure in a landscape defined by what is missing.

You walk toward it.

areaName: Luna: The Shepherd of the Grove
text:
A large figure is perched on a low-hanging limb of a massive oak.

She has four wings of equal size, arranged in two tiers along her back. The first pair sits high at her shoulders, with the second pair tucked neatly just beneath them. The feathers are thick and soft slate grey, layered for silent flight.

She has a sharply hooked beak. Her eyes are deep pools of dark, metallic mercury. She has fluffy tufts of feathers near her ears and thin mothlike antennae that flit as if on high alert.

On the tip of a wing, she cradles a single firefly that has gone still and dark.

She doesn't turn her head as you approach, but her voice is steady and clear. “You have returned to the grove, Inker. Your stride is firm. I can hear the weight of the deep earth in your steps.”

You look up at her, but there is no recognition. “I don't remember you,” you say. “I don't remember being here before.”

She finally turns her head to look down at you, the mercurial pools of her eyes reflecting nothing. A resolved stillness settles over her.

“Then the Unmaking has reached deeper than I feared. It is an unfortunate thing to lose one's own story. I am Luna. I am the shepherd of these oaks and the creatures within them. I have spent my life learning their needs so I could meet them.”

She looks back toward the infinite sky above the trees. “It has gone dark. I have called to the stars every hour since the Unmaking took the light, but there is no answer. They have stopped their part of the conversation. I cannot fix a dark this deep on my own.”

She swoops down from the branch, landing silently on the path. She extends her wing toward you, offering the fragile firefly resting in her feathers. It looks as dull as a piece of charcoal.

“This one is fading. Its light is gone. Take it into your hands so it can feel yours. I will speak to it until its spark returns. Come, we have work to do.”

As you accept the small, dark creature, Luna beats her wings, lifting gracefully off the ground. Her movement is fluid and soundless.

The beating of her four wings shift slightly to adjust to your pace as the two of you begin to walk deeper into the ancient oaks.

You cup your hands together, holding the dark, lifeless firefly into your palms. It weighs almost nothing, like a dried leaf.

As the small, dark form settles, you feel the deep chill within it.

Luna leans in. The sound she makes is a sequence of low, melodic clicks and soft, sustained hums that vibrate through your fingers. It is a deep resonance, a sound urging the tiny insect to find the light within.

For a long moment, there is only the gentle swaying of the oak branches above and the rhythmic vibration of Luna's voice. You watch the dark insect. A single leg twitches against your palm—a small sign of life. But the firefly stays dark. Luna stops the sound.

She looks at the insect, her mercurial eyes darkening even more. “The Unmaking has reached the center of its spark,” she says. “It has fallen dark, forgotten how to glow. It will take more than a momentary spark to rekindle its fire.”

She reaches out and takes the firefly back, tucking it carefully into the feathers of one of her wings. “We will keep it close. The work is difficult, but the light must still be out there. We just have to be determined enough to find it.”

She gestures forward with a slight tilt of her head, her antennae flicking as she scans the path ahead.

Luna takes flight once again. You walk beside her, the soft crunch of the lichen under your feet the only sound under the starless sky.

Luna circles slowly overhead, her wings barely disturbing the brisk air. The trunks of the oaks below her look like pillars against the featureless black of the sky. Mid-circle, she angles her wing to whisper to the frail firefly nestled in her feathers, then looks back up into the void.

“I cannot be everywhere at once,” she says. “No shepherd can. So, I found other eyes.”

She nods toward the vacant sky. “We named them together—the stars. Not by the names on the old maps. We gave them our own, you and I. And once they had names, I gave each constellation a post. A part of the forest to watch over. When something was wrong, they told me.”

She glides into a slow turn above the canopy. You follow below, stepping carefully in the pitch black.

Luna is still above you, her wings tracing slow arcs between the reaching oaks.

“We found Flicker first,” she says, nodding towards the sky above Thistlewick Thicket, where Flicker reminded you of your name. “An oblong shape with four bright lines trailing behind it, like his tails when he runs. Quick to notice. Quick to react. It suited him.” She tilts her wing briefly, checking the firefly and murmuring softly, then levels out. “I asked that constellation to watch over the thicket when I could not.”

You and Luna look up toward the sky, searching for even a faint flicker of light between the leaves, as you continue through the gnarled oaks.

Luna drifts lower as a draft moves through the canopy, rustling the paper-thin leaves. She gestures with her wing towards the empty sky hanging over the Wandering River, where Pebble reminded you of how you saw the world.

“Pebble came next,” she says. “A round shape sitting low on a long stream of stars, like she was floating on her back down the river. I asked that constellation to watch over the valley.” She turns in a slow arc and bends her head toward the wing holding the delicate firefly, speaking to it in a hushed tone. A look of concern flashes across her face, and she picks up speed, beating her wings more urgently.

You stay close behind as the path curves gently through the trees.

The oaks press closer together here, their contorted limbs reaching overhead in tangled arcs. Luna moves through them without slowing, dodging branches with practiced ease.

“Gully came next,” she says, looking at the deep void over the Glowcap Marsh, where Gully reminded you of your place in the world. “We found a wide, low shape with three stars set side by side at the center. The middle one sat where his third eye would be.” She swirls around a large trunk, and the motion brings her wing close enough that she murmurs something inaudible to the snuffed-out firefly before heading on. “That constellation watched over the marsh.”

You continue forward, the shadows of the trees pressing close around the path.

Luna has climbed higher again, her silhouette just visible against the dark canopy. The grove is quieter here, the reaching limbs of the oaks so dense overhead that the sky is barely visible between them.

“Mica was the last one we found,” she says, and you look back the way you had just come, toward the deep nothingness above the Crystal Caverns, where Mica reminded you of your potential. “An even shape with two long arcs opening from it like wings in motion. Precise. Symmetrical. It could not have belonged to anyone else.”

She descends slightly, her lower wings slowing as she passes close overhead, and speaks to the darkened firefly with a growing urgency. “That constellation watched over the caverns. Every shift in the stone, every change in the atmosphere—it recorded all of it. The most thorough watcher I had.”

The path softens beneath your feet, the ancient lichen muffling your steps. Luna rises again, resuming her wide arc through the dark.

Luna has grown quieter as you walk, her speed steadily increasing, her whispers to the extinguished firefly tucked safely in her wing becoming more frequent, her antennae flicking more frantically. Though her face remains calm, the beat of her wings steady.

“We never finished,” she says solemnly, her antennae drooping. “There was still one part of the forest without eyes. We kept looking but had not yet found them when the Unmaking came.”

A shiver runs through you. She continues, “Now I cannot find any of the guardians. I have searched the dark over and over, looking for even the slightest trace of their light. Called to them in the night and listened for even the faintest whisper of a response. But they are gone. Completely gone.”

You feel their absence now, as Luna does. It's almost as if you have lost the creatures themselves, the friends who gave back what you had forgotten, who guided you when you were lost.

But there is still one more out there—the final friend you never found in the stars. Somewhere in this undone world, in the one part of the forest that had no eyes watching over it, someone has been waiting. Keeping whatever they kept of you.

You and Luna continue forward into the dark, your heart heavy and aching, but with a flicker of something that might, in another world, have been called hope.

Between the reaching oaks, you watch Luna tend to the lifeless firefly—occasionally whispering something you cannot hear, and could not understand even so.

“The stars screamed when it happened,” she says, her voice steady, but with a rising tension beneath the surface. “All of them, at once. Every constellation I had ever spoken to. I heard them cry out across the whole sky. And then silence. The dark came down—the Unmaking. They have not answered since.”

She flies on, her rhythm unbroken. “I will keep calling to them. It is the only thing I know how to do.”

You walk beneath her in silence, the weight of what she carries settling over you like the darkness.

Luna drifts down toward the canopy and hovers at the level of the highest branches, one wing resting lightly against the bark of a massive oak. The tree is so large its top is lost in the darkness, its surface dry and rough.

“The roots are quieter than they used to be,” she says. “But they are still speaking.” She lifts her wing and looks down at you, her mercury eyes reflecting nothing but the path ahead. “I taught you to listen once. You pressed your palms to the bark and stood so still. After a long while, you felt it. Not words. Something slower. A deep patience passing through the wood like a heartbeat.”

She tilts her head, her antennae fluttering as she catches a shift in the air. “The oaks remember you. Even now, under this starless sky, they lean in when you pass. Living things do that sometimes. They remember your touch.”

You look at the row of ancient trunks lining the path. In the dim light, the trees seem to loom closer, their heavy limbs bowing toward the center of the road. You continue deeper into the grove, the air growing warmer.

Luna alights briefly on a high branch, looking out over a wide clearing between the oaks. Her wings settle around her, the dark firefly still tucked securely between the downy feathers of her wing.

“On warm nights, we used to sit in the tallest oak and watch the fireflies rise out of the grass,” she says. “Thousands of them. All at once. They drifted upward until the whole grove was full of light. They looked like stars brought down to earth.”

She reaches into her feathers, checking the dark insect. Its legs twitch weakly, a faint sign of life maintained by her proximity. “On the best nights, they rose high enough to meet the stars above. Sky and earth together as points of light. You could not tell where one ended and the other began.”

She lifts off the branch without another word, her four wings beating rhythmically as she ascends back into the dark canopy. You walk through the silent clearing below her, the grass pale and still beneath your feet.

The path descends into a wide, shallow bowl of earth where the oaks grow densest. Their limbs arch overhead in great, contorted reaches, straining toward a light that’s no longer there, their silver-grey bark rough against the dark. The ground between their roots is thick with shadow.

Luna drifts low, her lower wings searching the gaps between the roots. “They are here,” she says. She draws three fireflies from a crevice with careful precision, their legs moving slowly against her feathers. “The Unmaking reached them too. They have no light left within them.”

She rises back toward the canopy, and you follow the path deeper into the bowl.

Luna descends toward another gap between the roots and looks down at you, her mercurial eyes steady. “Help me,” she says. “The ones near the base. They need your touch.” You kneel in the dark and gather the small, lightless bodies one by one, cupping them carefully against your palms.

She watches until you stand. “Hold them close,” she says quietly. “They need what the Unmaking took from them. We have to help them get it back.” Then she beats her wings and rises, and you walk out of the hollow together.

The path climbs out of the bowl, the ground beneath your feet turning to pale, powdery dust. The oaks thin here, their roots shallower, their reach less desperate. The cold settles more openly without the canopy to hold it in. Luna sweeps wide above you, her form dissolving into the starless sky.

You cup your hands closer to your chest and press onward, doing what you can for the small, still bodies resting against your palms.

The oaks close in again, their contorted limbs arching so low the path becomes a tunnel of iron-grey wood. They do not droop—they reach, hard and insistent, frozen mid-extension toward something overhead that never came. You move through them in a crouch, the dry friction of wood filling the silence.

Luna threads the gaps ahead of you, her wings adjusting with fluid precision. She says nothing. You follow the pale shimmer of her feathers through the dark.

Luna hovers near a massive, twisted trunk, her lower wings spread wide against the bark. Her throat pulses with a low, constant thrum that travels through the soles of your feet and up into your chest. You wait, watching.

A slow creak answers her—a single branch shifting upward, straightening almost imperceptibly. Luna turns to you, her antennae trembling. “They are still trying,” she says. “That is enough.”

She lifts back into the canopy, and you press on beneath the dark arms of the wood.

Luna stops speaking entirely. She produces a sequence of low clicks and a sustained hum as she moves through the interlocking branches above, a silver shape just visible in the dark. You can feel the faint movement of the fireflies’ legs against your palms—small, intermittent, persisting.

You keep your head down and follow the rhythm of her wings. The air is now warm as a summer's day. The trees press closer on either side, their reaching limbs motionless and vast.

You match her pace, looking straight ahead.

The path opens into a small clearing where the oaks pull back from one another, their reaching limbs no longer interlocked. Luna slows, her wingbeats changing rhythm. She descends toward the base of a broad trunk and stops.

Tucked into a hollow at its roots, three fireflies glow dimly. Faint, barely a suggestion of light, but steady. The Unmaking did not reach them here, or did not reach them fully. Luna is motionless for a long moment, studying them. Then she looks at you, something resolved and quiet in her expression.

“This is where I stay,” she says. “These fireflies still have their spark. If anything can reach the others, it is them.” She settles at the hollow’s edge, drawing dozens of dark, lifeless fireflies from her feathers and placing them carefully beside the glowing ones.

She nods at you, signaling you to do the same. You set the tiny insects you’ve been carrying gently amongst the others. “Go on, {{characterName}}. You have what you came for. So do I.” She does not watch you leave. She is already working, her low clicks and hums filling the hollow.

You step back onto the path and continue alone into the dark.

The grove thins and the darkness thins with it. The light here is sharp and relentless, pouring down from a sun that gives nothing. No warmth reaches the ground. The wildflowers along the path have folded in on themselves, their petals shrunk and papery, their stems bowed over as if cowering from the sun. The grass is pale, brittle, and broken. The trees at the forest's edge are small and shriveled, their branches bare and contracted tight, as if curling away from the very light they once grew toward. Everything here had the chance to bloom and turned away from it.
You shield your eyes against the brightness and press on.

You find a nugget of polished metal buried in a dry, cracked crater surrounded by wilting reeds. Its surface is marred by deep, frantic scratches. You picture someone standing over the water, trying to obscure their own reflection because they couldn't stand the sight of themselves—someone who was too ashamed to shine. You wipe away the silt and put the chunk of metal in your pocket. It feels cold against your skin, sending a chill through you.

You near the edge of the grove, trees giving way to withering wildflowers. Your hands are empty now, the fireflies left behind in the hollow. But something Luna said won't leave you. We found them in the stars. You look up at the dark sky—at the places where the stars used to be. And you understand, suddenly, that you must have loved these creatures very much. You loved them in the way you love something you can't stop thinking about when it isn't there. You looked up at the dark on nights when you were far from the thicket, far from the river, far from the marsh and the caverns. And far from the grove. You searched the stars for them until you found them anyway. You carried them with you wherever you went—stitched into the dark overhead, so they’d always be with you. You belonged here. Not just to this forest, but to the creatures in it. They were yours, and you were theirs. And now everything is gone, your memories ripped from you like the stars from the sky. But you are still walking, still moving forward, and the dark above feels less like absence now and more like a map waiting for you to rediscover it—a map of everything worth finding again

The trees give way to open sky, the canopy dissolving into pale, blinding expanse. The path widens. The air has a noticeable, dry heat, having been stripped of the cool dampness of the grove.
As the last of the grove falls behind you, the pull in your bones has shifted again. It feels more determined now—more deliberate.

You are no longer following a blind beckoning toward the heart of the forest. Step by step, you are going there yourself. You will find what stole the light for the friend who never let you succumb to the darkness.
You hesitate for a moment and then step out of the trees and into the open.

The grove falls away behind you, and the world opens.

The meadow stretches in every direction, vast and unbroken. It should be beautiful—you can tell it was, once. The grass grows thick and waist-high, and the wildflowers are still there if you look closely, their shapes intact. But every stem is bowed. Every petal faces down. Nothing here reaches upward. The whole meadow leans away from the sun as if the light is something to shrink from.

The air smells of dry chalk and something faintly sweet, like flowers that have been pressed between pages for too long.

Far across the plateau, at the edge of where the meadow meets a line of withered trees, something stands. The figure is too still to be a trick of the light. The presence is watching you.

You start walking.

areaName: The Horned One: The Clarion Call
text:
The first thing you see is the gold.

It catches the sterile light from across the plateau—two branching points of warm color rising above the bowed grass, splitting and splitting against the pale sky like the last living thing in the world. You have not seen color since you first woke at the forest’s edge. Your eyes do not know what to do with it.

The antlers rise from the creature’s head like golden branches, tines splitting and splitting again. The texture is less like bone and more like the bark of every tree the creature has ever known. Golden leaves adorn the tines and shimmer in the light.

As you draw closer, the creature takes shape beneath the antlers. The Horned One is tall, possessing the sturdy frame of something built for strength and long distances. The creature stands as if rooted, lanky legs ending in broad, cloven hooves firmly planted in earth.

The coat is the color of dried grass, a shade that would have made the form nearly invisible against the meadow...once. The creature’s face is long and calm, featuring dark, unblinking eyes with a gaze that seems to hold everything.

This is the only remaining warmth that the Unmaking did not erase.

The Horned One does not greet you. When the creature speaks, it is as if the conversation has been underway for some time.

“You stopped at the edge of the grove,” the voice says. It is low and resonant, a sound that seems to rise from the earth rather than a throat. “You stood there for a long moment. I watched you decide.”

The creature stares at you, dark eyes unblinking.

“That is the only memory of yours that concerns me. Not what you have lost. What you chose to do at the edge of it.”

You say nothing.

“Good. You are already listening. That is a start.”

The Horned One turns toward the open meadow. You fall into step beside the creature, the golden antlers catching the light ahead of you.

The Horned One does not move from the shadow of the withered tree. Golden antlers catch the sterile light as the creature speaks.

“This meadow grew toward a sun it decided it did not deserve,” the creature says. “So it stopped. Folded itself down. Made itself small so the world could not say it had no right to stand tall.”

A pause. The dry stalks shift without wind, as if pulling inward.

“You have hesitated the same way. Twice that I recorded. Once at the northern edge of the thicket, before the steepest grade, where you slowed until I thought you had stopped entirely. Once at the mouth of the caverns, where you stood in the dark for eleven counted breaths.”

The creature’s dark eyes find you.

“But I am not here to discuss the hesitation. I am here because of what came after it. Both times, you moved. That is the only part of your history worth carrying into what comes next.”

The creature moves forward, sure and deliberate, and you walk alongside.

“You tell me you do not remember who you are.”

The Horned One takes one slow step toward you. The pale grass bends and does not spring back.

“I tell you: That does not matter. Your feet carried you through the thicket. Through the river valley. Through the rot of the marsh and the dark of the cave. Through the starless sky of the grove. You did not remember yourself through any of it, and yet here you stand.”

The creature stops.

“The forgetting did not stop you. It tried. It failed. That is the only biography that matters now—not what you were, but what you did when you could not remember what you were. I have kept that record.” A pause. “It is the record of someone who does not stop.”

You look at the bowed flowers at your feet. Not one of them is looking back.

“Your feet remember the road. Your chest remembers the breath of the high air. That is enough. I do not ask for your history—I ask for your momentum.” The Horned One’s dark eyes look down at the folded buttercups. “Do not do what they did. Do not decide you have no right to keep going. Stand tall, Inker.”

The Horned One moves forward without looking back. You lift your eyes from the flowers and follow.

“The stars have gone dark,” the Horned One says. “The paths have turned to ash. In such a world, the only direction left is the one you carry inside.”

The golden antlers cast no shadow in the sterile light.

“Your heart is a needle, Inker. It does not heed the dark, and it does not fear the cold. It only knows one word.” The dark eyes drop briefly to your chest, then rise again. “Do not look to the sky for guidance. The stars have abdicated their posts. Do not look to the path for the way. It can only lead you so far. Look inward. Your resolve is a needle that only points one way. Align your spirit to it and let the world follow your lead.”

The meadow is dead silent.

“You will know the word. And when you do, remember it. You will need it before the end.”

The creature walks on. You keep pace, a space sitting in your chest where the word will sit.

“There is one more thing.”

The stillness around the Horned One shifts. The dark eyes carry something new—the weight of something that demands to be met honestly.

“The Unmaking is a vast, hungry silence, but it is not absolute. It can be pushed back by every determined step. Resolve is not a feeling—it is a choice you make with every mile. Do not look at the shadows flickering at the edge of your vision. Look at the path you are treading into existence. Resolve is the one thing the Unmaking cannot touch.”

The creature is very still.

“At the heart of this forest, you will meet someone. I must warn you: Do not arrive there small. Do not arrive uncertain. Do not arrive still carrying the destruction of the forest inside of you.” The gaze does not waver. “You will need every mile you have walked to stand in that place. Every moment you chose to move forward over stopping. Every step you took when the world gave you no reason to keep going.”

A long pause.

“Prepare yourself.”

The Horned One is still for a long moment. Then the creature turns, and you understand the conversation is nearly over.

The Horned One turns away—not toward the heart of the forest, but back the way you came. Back toward the grove, back toward the dark of the cave and the rot and the river and the thicket. The golden antlers catch the light one last time. The creature’s voice rings out. Resonant. Certain. “The horizon is not a place to stop, Inker—it is a reminder that there is more to discover. The Unmaking has obscured the paths, but it cannot steal the ground beneath your feet. I have set the coordinate in your heart. My eyes will be on the horizon we have yet to reach, but my command remains in the marrow of your bones. When the cold tries to slow your blood, remember the North I have given you. Do not look back for me. Look forward for the light. You will carry the name of every creature with you.” A pause. “You did not walk here alone {{characterName}}. You will not walk forward alone. Every name you were given in these woods is yours to keep. Mine is the last. I am Harken. I told you that you would know the word. Here it is…” Harken’s dark eyes hold you one last time, brief and absolute. “Move.” Harken bounds back into the pale grass without looking back. The creature fades from view within minutes. The golden antlers are the last thing you see—splitting and splitting against the bleached sky—and then they are gone too. The silence that follows is not empty. It has a shape to it. A direction. As the meadow closes behind you, the coordinate in your chest does not waver. The pull in your bones has changed—it is no longer a pull at all. It is a push, steady and insistent, from somewhere behind your sternum. You turn toward the heart of the forest and walk—for the one who kept the record of every time you chose to move, and who never once doubted you.

The path beneath your feet disappears, swallowed by a sea of waist-high grass. Stiff and skeletal, the stalks are coated in a fine, white powder that kicks up like salt with every step. They stand petrified, as if sensing the end is near. There is no wind, yet the meadow is never silent. Every step produces a papery rustling that carries for miles in the thin air. You feel small here. The pale sky feels like a watching eye that never blinks. You think about Harken's words. At the heart of this forest, you will meet someone. . . . Do not arrive there small.You straighten your spine, lift your chest, hold your head high, and keep walking.

The light is a paradox. It is so bright that the world is reduced to sharp lines and the deepest charcoal shadows, illuminating the landscape without revealing it. You hold your hand up to the sun, and the light passes through the gaps of your fingers without casting a shadow to shield your eyes. You look down at the smudge of ink on your skin. In this bleached landscape, it is the only thing that looks substantial. The meadow feels like a ghost of a place, a memory that has been scrubbed clean until only the armature remains. Do not arrive uncertain, Harken said. You are not certain. You have not been certain once since you woke at the edge of the forest. But you are still here, still moving forward, still putting one foot in front of the other. You wonder if that's what certainty really is—choosing something over and over in the absence of any guarantee that you're right. You let that thought continue to carry you forward.

Distance is difficult to judge in the open. There are no landmarks to mark your progress or measure yourself against. You find a cluster of rocks that look like they were once part of a stream, but the bed is filled with nothing but silt. You stop to catch your breath. You look up at the pale line where the earth meets the sky. The horizon is not a place to stop, Inker—it is a reminder that there is more to discover. You fix your gaze on it and press on.

You stop to rest and your pack slides from your shoulders with a weight that surprises you.

You open it.

The thorn. The dry leaf it pierced. The knotted vine, still unyielding, still wound impossibly tight against itself. The leaden root with the metal nugget grown into its heart. The worry stone, its groove worn smooth by a thumb that rubbed and rubbed until the rock gave way. The piece of white bark with the scratched-out figure.

You have been carrying all of it since the beginning. Each one found in the margins of the path, pressed into your hands by some instinct you couldn’t name. You told yourself you were imagining the person who left them. You pictured a stranger. Someone driven by a rage with nowhere to go. Someone drowning in their own weight. Someone fearing they were truly, fundamentally alone.

Now, on the far side of Harken’s warning, you wonder for the first time if they were left by the one waiting at the heart of the forest.

You reach for the metal nugget last. You have held it before—cold, scratched into ruin by someone who couldn’t bear to look at themselves.

It is no longer cold.

You turn it over in your palm. Where the frantic scratches caught the sterile light before, they catch something warmer now. Where you held the nugget, the grey has shifted—scrubbed away, or transmuted—and beneath it, unmistakably, is gold.

You close your hand around it and hold it for a long moment.

Then you place it back with the others, shoulder the pack, and keep walking.

The grass begins to thin, revealing a wide, flat plateau of cracked earth. The heart of the forest darkens the horizon ahead.

You think of Harken’s words about the hesitations recorded, the moments of stopping and then choosing forward. You have been adding to that record with every step since the parting.

The heart of the forest is somewhere beyond the tree line. You will reach it in time. For now there is only the next step, and the next, and the certainty that both are enough.

You do not slow.

You've come to realize that there is nothing left to find here. No creatures watching from the grass. No objects half-buried in the silt. No conversations waiting to be had. This part of meadow offers only the ground beneath your feet, the sky above, and the thoughts in your head. All of them are the color and texture of a canvas scraped clean. The tree line ahead has grown from a suggestion into a wall. Dark and dense, the trunks are barely visible from here. The canopy is a ceiling that begins where the sky ends. Something is in there, waiting. Prepare yourself. Harken’s words have not left you. But how do you prepare yourself for something you know nothing about? All you're sure of is this—what waits at the heart of this forest will require everything you have. You take stock of everything you have. Everything you've become since you stepped onto the path at the forest's edge. It is more than you started with. Your step does not falter. You walk into the trees.

The meadow ends. The cracked earth gives way to something older—dark soil, dense and damp. The smell of it rises around you, familiar, like an old memory you can't quite place. The withered grass is finally behind you. Ahead, the trees are ancient things, their trunks as wide as boulders, their bark scored with deep lines that run in patterns too deliberate to be accidental. Above the canopy, the jagged peak of the mountain stands tall. The coordinate in your chest does not waver. You are closer now. You can feel it. You stand at the threshold and look into deep, dense woods. Somewhere in there, the Unmaking began. Somewhere in there, someone is waiting. Somewhere in there, lies the answer to a question you do not yet know to ask. You move.
